title: Anthropic posts $80B loss in first half of 2026
content:
Anthropic posts $80bn loss in first half of 2026: WSJ
The loss is up $13 billion more than last year, driven by accounting charges, the report said.
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company known for creating the chatbot Claude, recorded a net loss of more than $80bn in the first half of 2026, according to the Wall Street Journal, as the market anticipates its looming initial public offering (IPO).
The corporation also indicated it could spend up to $750bn in coming years to acquire more computing capacity, including potential deals currently under discussion, the Journal said on Tuesday.
The main driver for the loss was the $72bn in accounting charges related to changes in the value of convertible notes and other financial instruments Anthropic issued to raise funding, the report said.
The loss figure was up from $13bn a year earlier, according to a draft prospectus, a legal document corporations submit to financial regulators, for its IPO.
The figures show the hefty costs of the AI race, even as investors look more closely at whether the money companies are pouring into chips and data centres will pay off.
Anthropic also shared a list of potential risk factors, including uncertainty over how to prevent its products from doing harm, whether through sophisticated cyberattacks or blackmail by uncontrolled models.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment, and the report on the non-public information could not be immediately verified.
Investors weigh loss
Reuters first reported in September that Anthropic posted a net loss of $42bn in 2025, as part of a series of exclusives from its IPO prospectus.
The company has benefited from the popularity of Claude Code, its coding assistant that developers use to write software and build apps.
But some current and prospective investors who attended Anthropic’s investor day in San Francisco, California, last week are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, four people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The investors who attended the event discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, three of the people said, a significant step down from the roughly $2 trillion valuation previously expected for the November share sale.
Anthropic’s revenue jumped to $16.3bn in the six-month period that ended June 30, up from $1.1bn a year ago, while AI infrastructure spending nearly quadrupled to almost $9bn, the Journal reported.
Anthropic reported last week that AI could be months away from learning to self-replicate on everyday home devices.

report.summary: Anthropic reportedly posted an $80bn net loss in H1 2026 on accounting charges, while eyeing up to $750bn in compute spending ahead of its IPO.
report.background: Anthropic, maker of Claude, has grown rapidly on enterprise AI and coding tools such as Claude Code, but the capital-intensive nature of frontier AI is reshaping its financial profile. The reported loss reflects both real spending and accounting volatility: convertible notes and other instruments used to raise money can swing sharply in value, creating large non-cash charges. It comes as Anthropic prepares for an IPO, a moment that forces previously private AI economics into public view. Rivals are also pouring billions into chips and data centers, and investors are increasingly asking whether revenue growth can justify the scale of compute commitments. The draft prospectus disclosure, including a possible $750bn future compute outlay, underscores how AI labs are making long-dated infrastructure bets even while current losses widen. The figures also arrive amid debate over AI safety risks and whether valuations for private AI companies have run ahead of fundamentals.
key_points: The $80bn net loss was mainly driven by $72bn in accounting charges tied to convertible notes and other financial instruments Anthropic used to raise funding. That means the headline loss is not simply cash burned on operations; it reflects how complex fundraising structures are valued. Still, it highlights the financial complexity behind private AI fundraising.

Revenue rose to $16.3bn in the six months ending June 30, up from $1.1bn a year earlier, while AI infrastructure spending nearly quadrupled to almost $9bn. The growth shows strong demand for Anthropic’s models and Claude Code, but it also shows how much compute capacity is needed to serve that demand.

Anthropic reportedly indicated it could spend up to $750bn in coming years on computing capacity, including deals under discussion. That is a staggering forward commitment for an AI lab, signaling that access to chips and data centers is now a core competitive battleground and a major source of financial risk.

Investors at Anthropic’s investor day discussed a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion previously expected for the November IPO. The lower range suggests financiers are reassessing AI valuations after seeing losses, spending plans, and the uncertain payoff from massive infrastructure investments.

The draft prospectus reportedly lists risk factors including uncertainty over preventing products from causing harm through cyberattacks or blackmail by uncontrolled models. Anthropic also said AI could be months away from learning to self-replicate on everyday home devices, adding safety and regulatory questions to its business story.
report.impact: The disclosure could become a reference point for how public markets price frontier AI labs. If Anthropic’s IPO lands below earlier expectations, other AI companies may face tougher questions about losses, compute commitments, and paths to profitability. For developers, continued investment in Claude and Claude Code is likely, but access terms and pricing may be tied more tightly to revenue and infrastructure costs. For regular users, the immediate effect may be limited, though the debate over safety risks—cyber misuse, model autonomy, and self-replication—could lead to stricter safeguards and more cautious product rollouts. The bigger signal is that the AI race is entering a phase where spending discipline and investor patience matter as much as model capability.
report.tools: To follow the AI-coding and cost story, try Claude Code and open-source coding agents such as Aider, Cline, Continue, and OpenHands. For local inference and experimentation, look at Ollama and vLLM; for tracking model risks and evaluations, explore LangSmith, Weights & Biases, and Inspect. IPO prospectus updates and Anthropic’s safety publications are worth monitoring.
